titel: The Battle Over Black Representation in the South

einzeiler: How the gutting of the Voting Rights Act and redistricting are transforming the South
kurzfassung: The weakening of the Voting Rights Act and aggressive redistricting by Republican legislatures are reshaping the political landscape of the American South. In states like Mississippi, Tennessee, and Louisiana, redrawn maps threaten Black political representation by breaking up Democratic strongholds. While this has sparked anger and widespread mobilization among voters and activists, it also risks deepening voter apathy as the midterms approach.
stichpunkte: The 1965 Voting Rights Act historically protected Black voting access and representation across the South.
Recent Supreme Court decisions have weakened the act, making it harder to prove intentional discrimination.
Southern Republican legislatures have seized on this shift to aggressively redraw congressional and state maps.
In Tennessee, Memphis was carved up into three districts, turning a Democratic stronghold into safe Republican territory.
Activists in Georgia and South Carolina successfully pushed back against redistricting plans, halting changes temporarily.
Mississippi has become a focal point, with packed hearings drawing intense opposition from residents and youth organizers.
Despite local outrage and packed protest hearings, Republicans are expected to maintain control over the new maps.
A competitive Senate race in Mississippi offers a test of whether voter frustration can translate into higher turnout.

clips.text: A court ruling tied to the Voting Rights Act enabled Alabama to elect two Black representatives simultaneously for the first time in history.

clips.hook: Carving up Memphis into conservative districts
clips.text: Lawmakers divided Memphis into multiple parts and combined them with rural white areas, turning a reliable Democratic stronghold into districts that favored Donald Trump.

clips.hook: Fighting the same fight as a generation ago
clips.text: An older resident describes being 69 years old and standing up to protest the same voting battles that his father had to fight.

clips.hook: Should have let sleeping dogs lie
clips.text: An elderly organizer warns that lawmakers made a mistake by provoking voters and waking up a dormant political movement.
A political figure argues that federal officials intentionally try to make citizens feel isolated and stripped of their influence.

beschreibung:
The approach to this year’s midterms has brought two hugely consequential changes to voting for Black Americans: the gutting of the Voting Rights Act, and redistricting. In the wake of those actions, efforts are underway to mobilize Black voters in the South.
In Mississippi, the Senate battle is being seen as a sleeper race, and the Black Democrat running has a chance of flipping the seat, but state lawmakers are trying to redraw the maps and do away with their one majority Black district.
Today, Emily Cochrane, a reporter covering the American South for The New York Times, addresses the implications for voters across the region — not just in the midterms, but for years to come.
Guest: Emily Cochrane, a national reporter for The New York Times covering the American South.
Background reading:
Black Democratic candidates running in the South have implored Black voters to go to the polls in response to the gutting of the Voting Rights Act.
High-profile Democrats across the country have some hope in Scott Colom’s bid for a seat in the Senate.
